opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to a pretty simple principle: you should assume the agent's sandbox is going to be compromised eventually. Not because the model is malicious, but because the sandbox is exactly where all the untrusted stuff lands. The agent is reading web pages, pulling in dependencies, running code it just wrote, processing documents that someone else authored. Any of those can carry a prompt injection or just a buggy script that dumps environment variables to a log. If your API keys and credentials live in that same space, then the blast radius of any one of those failures is everything.

So with the harness, the way we think about it is that the agent should be able to *use* a capability without ever *holding* the secret behind it. The secret store sits outside, and the harness acts as a broker. When the agent wants to call, say, a GitHub API or hit a database, the request goes through the harness, which attaches the credential on the way out. The model sees the result, but the token itself never enters its context window and never touches the sandbox filesystem. That matters a lot, because once a secret is in the context, you've basically lost control of where it can end up. It can get echoed into a commit message, a summary, a tool call to some other service.

The other piece is policy and auditability. If secrets go through a separate broker, you get a single choke point where you can scope things. This task gets read access to one repo for the next twenty minutes, and that's it. You can log every use, revoke instantly, and rotate without rebuilding the sandbox. If the secrets are just sitting in the sandbox as env vars, you've given up all of that granularity.

And honestly, it also makes the sandbox more disposable, which is what you want. If something looks off, you just throw the whole environment away and spin up a fresh one, and you haven't leaked anything of lasting value. Keeping those two concerns separate is what lets you be aggressive about giving the agent freedom inside the box, because the stuff you actually care about protecting isn't in there.

r001.rationale: It says credentials stored in the sandbox could be dumped or echoed elsewhere, making them available for exfiltration.

r002.rationale: It explains that the harness attaches credentials to outgoing requests while the token never enters the model’s context or sandbox filesystem.

fable-5.1.text:
So the simplest way I'd put it is: the agent should never be in a position where the thing it's running can read the thing it's authenticating with.

When you give an agent a sandbox, you're basically saying "here's a place where you can do whatever you want, run arbitrary code, install packages, shell out, and if it goes wrong we can throw the whole thing away." That's the right model. But the moment you drop an API key or an OAuth token into that same environment, you've undermined the whole point. Now the blast radius isn't the sandbox anymore, it's whatever that credential can reach. And the agent is executing code it wrote thirty seconds ago, based on a web page it just read. So prompt injection, a malicious dependency, even just an honest mistake like catting a dotenv file into the transcript, all of those become credential exfiltration paths.

So in Exo the split is: the secret store lives outside, in the harness process, and the sandbox only ever sees the result of an action, not the key that authorized it. If the agent wants to call GitHub, it asks the harness, the harness attaches the token, makes the call, and hands back the response. The model literally cannot print the secret because it was never in its address space.

There are a couple of nice second-order effects. One is auditing. Every privileged action goes through a single chokepoint, so you get a real log of "the agent used this credential to do this thing at this time," instead of trying to reconstruct it from shell history. Another is scoping. You can hand out narrow capabilities per task, like "read-only on this one repo," without the agent being able to escalate just because a broader token happened to be lying around. And honestly, it keeps us honest as the people building it, because it forces you to enumerate what the agent actually needs instead of giving it your whole environment and hoping.

The pushback I usually get is that it's slower or more annoying to wire up, and that's true, there's friction. But I think that friction is exactly where it should be. Giving an agent credentials should feel like a deliberate act, not something that happens by default because the sandbox inherited your shell.

r001.rationale: It says putting an API key or token in the sandbox creates credential-exfiltration paths, including through prompt injection or malicious code.

r002.rationale: It explains that the harness keeps the secret outside the sandbox, attaches it when making a requested call, and returns the result without exposing the key to the agent.

astra-6.text:
Because the agent’s sandbox is where it runs code, and you want to assume that code might do something you didn’t intend—whether that’s a mistake or the result of prompt injection. If the secrets live inside that sandbox, anything running there can potentially read them and send them somewhere else.

Keeping the secret store outside gives you a boundary you can enforce. The agent can request an operation that needs authentication, and the harness can authorize that operation and attach the credential without exposing the credential itself. So you’re giving the agent the ability to do a particular thing, rather than handing it a reusable key. That doesn’t eliminate every risk, but it makes a compromised sandbox much less damaging.

r001.rationale: The response says that secrets inside the sandbox could be read by code running there and sent elsewhere.

r002.rationale: It says the harness can authorize an operation and attach the credential without exposing the credential to the agent.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the agent’s sandbox is where it runs code, and you should assume that code can read anything you put there. If you put credentials in the sandbox, a prompt injection or an untrusted dependency can potentially extract them.

Keeping the secret store outside gives the harness a separate boundary. The agent can request an operation that needs a credential, and the harness can check whether that operation is allowed and attach the credential without exposing the raw secret to the agent. You still have to constrain those operations, but you’ve reduced the chance that one compromised execution turns into a credential leak.

r001.rationale: It says code in the sandbox can read anything placed there and that credentials there could be extracted by prompt injection or an untrusted dependency.

r002.rationale: It explains that the harness can attach a credential for an allowed operation without exposing the raw secret to the agent.
